analysis.title: Election Watch 2026: 10 key questions on the US midterms
key_insights: UBS CIO expects the 2026 midterms to produce divided government. Senate rules, party divisions, the presidential veto and already wide federal deficits constrain sweeping policy changes.
Election odds: 50% Democrats win both chambers, 40% Democrats win the House while Republicans keep the Senate, 10% Republicans keep both. Majority size depends on election-night results.

Democratic Senate control would shift committee leadership, investigations, nominations and judicial confirmations, and would open a path to budget reconciliation, though the Senate rules, party divisions and the veto would still limit legislation.

A result that differs meaningfully from expectations could move market-implied odds for the 2028 presidency. A strong Democratic showing raises the odds of a Democratic president, and a Republican sweep extends the current policy agenda.

Divided government and wide deficits likely rule out another large fiscal package like the 2025 tax law. Social Security's projected 2032 trust-fund depletion raises the importance of reform, and a likely compromise relies more on new revenue (for example, payroll tax on earnings above current limits) than on benefit cuts.

A 2027 debt-ceiling agreement could soften scheduled social-program cuts and raise defense spending, which would reverse the expected narrowing of deficits and add Treasury supply. A late deal could raise market volatility.

UBS still expects inflation to moderate, the Fed to finish raising rates and Treasury yields to settle lower. Current yields offer attractive income, but persistent deficits and heavy issuance support caution on the longest maturities.

The executive branch keeps broad tariff authority regardless of who controls Congress. Courts could constrain specific tariff authorities, Canada and Mexico focus on the USMCA review, and Asia watches technology controls.

Under divided government, House Democrats would likely increase oversight of AI companies, while the Senate's 60-vote threshold limits broad federal legislation. A narrower bipartisan package could speed data-center permitting, protect ratepayers and make developers bear more grid-upgrade costs.

UBS expects the AI buildout to continue because demand is strong, capital spending supports growth and earnings, and bipartisan support for technology investment makes a material slowdown unlikely. State and local rules will still shape project timing and location.

Midterm-year averages have limited value as trading signals. In 2026 stocks reached record highs on AI investment and profit growth despite the usual year-two weakness, while bond yields rose in the first half and volatility increased before the election.
Democrats could gain two to four governorships. Thirty-six governor races and 164 statewide ballot measures will shape taxes, housing, health care, education, energy and infrastructure.

Federal transfers provide roughly one-third of state revenue (20%-39% across states). Permanent Medicaid and safety-net cuts would force budget adjustments, with credit impact varying by federal dependence, while strong reserves, taxing authority, balanced-budget rules and phased implementation of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act should help. States could also cut funding to cities, schools, transit and hospitals, spreading pressure across the municipal market.

For long-term investors, growth, earnings, inflation and rates matter most. UBS expects growth and inflation to slow, the Fed to finish raising rates and yields to settle slightly lower in 2027, with strong earnings continuing to support equities.

sector_views.rationale: AI buildout expected to continue on strong demand and bipartisan support, despite possible oversight and local permitting friction.
Federal funding cuts could pressure state budgets and spread to cities, schools, transit and hospitals, but reserves, taxing authority and phased implementation support adjustment.

earnings_insights: Strong earnings will likely continue to support equities, per UBS CIO. No company-level figures are given.
